newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK leadership contenders grilled by China committee.
newsitem.headline: HK leadership contenders grilled by China committee.

text.p: Candidates vying to lead Hong Kong after Britain departs next year faced a volley of questions from the 400 members of a China-controlled committee when it launched a three-day vetting process on Wednesday.
The meeting of the Selection Committee, charged with finding a chief executive to succeed colonial governor Chris Patten, took place under heavy security.
It is the latest stage of a selection process that has cut the number of contenders for the leadership post to three. Hong Kong reverts to China in 16 days at midnight on June 30.

The meeting would give Selection Committee members an opportunity to get to know the candidates before they cast their votes on December 11, China's Hong Kong policy boss Lu Ping said in his opening address.
Each candidate was given 40 minutes to state their case in the morning session, before the start of questioning.

Shipping tycoon Tung Chee-hwa, who won a commanding 206 votes in the first-round ballot two weeks ago and has been tipped as Chinese President Jiang Zemin's favourite, said Hong Kong people had spent too much time bickering over transitional political issues and should start to look ahead.
The territory needed a long-term strategy to maintain its financial and trading supremacy in the 21st century, Tung said.
He was confident he could lead Hong Kong into the century as a compassionate, stable, equitable and wealthy society.

Hong Kong's former Chief Justice Ti Liang Yang, who came second in the first ballot with 82 votes but who has won the highest ratings from the public in popularity polls, said he would form a "moderate and rather conservative government".

Yang said his professional experience as a judge was his strong selling point. He told the selection board that he would run Hong Kong in conformity with the Basic Law, a post-1997 constitution for Hong Kong, as if presiding over a court case.
The third candidate, entrepreneur Peter Woo, who mustered only 54 votes in the first round, said he would not quit the race as suggested by some people who doubted his prospects.
Woo spoke out in defence of Western values, saying not all Western things were evil, in contrast to his two rivals who stressed Chinese values and culture.
"Hong Kong is based on the rule of law, which is a part of Western culture. The rule of law has to be maintained in order to ensure the long-term confidence of Hong Kong people," he said
A handful of pro-democracy demonstrators staged a non-violent protest outside the Hong Kong Convention Centre, the venue of the meeting and of next year's grand handover ceremony.
They branded the leadership contest as undemocratic and burned a black box symbolising the "darkness" in which the selection process was unfolding without the participation of Hong Kong's electorate.
Lu, as has often occurred on his visits to Hong Kong, dodged protesters by leaving the airport by a side door after his arrival. He avoided them again at the conference centre.

Scores of riot police were trucked into the area before dawn on fears of there would be a repeat of the skirmishes that took place during the first meeting of the committee two weeks ago when protesters stormed into the building.
After failing to hand Lu a petition condemning the selection process, the protesters gave it to a committee member and set fire to the black box before leaving.
